The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) \\ y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y))=-\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x))=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi y) & -\pi x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi y) \\ \pi y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,1) & =|\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & -\pi (0)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (1)) \\ \pi (1)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (0)) & \operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi (0))\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ \pi  & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =(-1)\cdot 0-0\cdot \pi  \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

The system can be rewritten in matrix form as x′=\boldsymbolf(x) where x=[x(t)y(t)] and \boldsymbolf(x)=[xcos⁡(πy)ysin⁡(πx)].

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of \boldsymbolf(x).

In our case, we have the following:

J=|∂f1∂x∂f1∂y∂f2∂x∂f2∂y|

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

∂f1∂x=∂∂x(xcos⁡(πy))=cos⁡(πy),∂f1∂y=∂∂y(xcos⁡(πy))=−πxsin⁡(πy)∂f2∂x=∂∂x(ysin⁡(πx))=ycos⁡(πx),∂f2∂y=∂∂y(ysin⁡(πx))=sin⁡(πx)

Thus, we have

J=|cos⁡(πy)−πxsin⁡(πy)πycos⁡(πx)sin⁡(πx)|.

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium x∗=[01] to get

J(0,1)=|cos⁡(π(1))−π(0)sin⁡(π(1))π(1)cos⁡(π(0))sin⁡(π(0))|=|−10π0|=(−1)⋅0−0⋅π=0.

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is not almost linear at x∗.
